Annual or monthly subscriptions: chart the discount, the stopping date and the cash paid

Compare the cost of the same service across possible usage periods, then separate upfront cash, unused prepaid time and an explicitly assumed refund.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore annual prepayment versus monthly flexibility

Interactive planning lab

Monthly plan: total paid for selected use$240
Annual plan: cost after assumed refund$300
Annual cost advantage; negative means dearer-$60

Hypothetical all-in prices for the same service and one twelve-month contract, with no renewal. Annual price is paid before use. Monthly payments are made at the start of each used month; chart points show completed months. Use ends after the selected month, monthly billing stops without a fee, and any assumed pro-rata refund arrives then. Refund % is a sensitivity input, not a legal entitlement. No interest, borrowing, tax credit, service failure or value of features is modeled. Verify actual contract terms and applicable consumer rights.

The central idea

An annual discount depends on how much of the prepaid period you use and what is returned if you stop. Compare total cost and payment timing on the same service.

01

Start with the same service and a complete price

An annual plan can advertise a lower equivalent monthly price while asking for the whole year’s payment immediately. A monthly plan can cost more for a full year while allowing payments to stop earlier. Both statements can be true, so the useful comparison includes duration as well as the price label.

The default compares the same service at CAD 30 per month with CAD 300 paid upfront for twelve months. Prices are assumed all-in, including any applicable sales tax and mandatory charges. There is no free trial, joining fee, renewal or change in features. If actual packages differ, the price comparison needs a separate assessment of what each package provides.

The Canadian Office of Consumer Affairs’ contract guidance emphasizes understanding the agreement and notes the role of provincial and territorial consumer protection offices. This calculator supplies a set of hypothetical billing terms. Its refund input does not establish the contract’s enforceable cancellation terms or replace applicable consumer rights.

02

Put the annual discount in dollars

Twelve monthly payments of CAD 30 total CAD 360. The CAD 300 annual plan therefore costs CAD 60 less over a full year, assuming the service is used throughout and the two packages are otherwise identical. The price difference is about 16.67% of the monthly plan’s full-year cost.

That percentage uses CAD 360 as the denominator. Dividing CAD 60 by the CAD 300 annual price instead gives 20%, a different comparison. Keeping the denominator explicit prevents two correct calculations from appearing contradictory.

The equivalent CAD 25 per month on the annual plan is an allocation of CAD 300 across twelve months. It is not the cash debit each month. The cash-timing chart records CAD 300 at index zero, immediately after annual prepayment, while the monthly plan has made no charge at that index. Both plans are then compared through the same twelve-month window.

03

Find the point where duration changes the result

With no unused-time refund, the annual plan remains CAD 300 even if use stops early. Monthly cost is CAD 30 multiplied by the number of consecutive months used. Ten months therefore produces a tie at CAD 300. At eleven or twelve months, the annual plan is cheaper under these assumptions.

The selected stopping date is eight months. The monthly plan costs CAD 240 and the prepaid plan costs CAD 300. Annual prepayment is therefore CAD 60 more expensive in this case, despite offering a full-year discount. The displayed annual-cost advantage is negative CAD 60 because it is defined as monthly cost minus annual net cost.

The duration chart contains twelve separate stopping decisions. It is not a cumulative ledger for one customer, and its lines do not predict how long anyone will remain subscribed. A service used seasonally in disconnected months would require its own billing and reactivation rules; this tool uses one continuous block of use starting with month one.

04

Separate unused prepaid time from a refund

At eight months, two-thirds of the annual period has been used. A straight-line allocation assigns CAD 200 of the CAD 300 price to used months and CAD 100 to the four unused months. The stacked bar keeps the full upfront price visible while separating the portion assumed returned.

At the default 0% refund input, none of the CAD 100 unused portion returns. At 50%, the model returns CAD 50 at the end of month eight, lowering the annual net cost to CAD 250. At 100%, it returns CAD 100, lowering net cost to CAD 200. These are alternative contract assumptions, rather than statements of legal entitlement.

A refund can change ultimate cost without removing the original cash requirement. Even in the 100% example, CAD 300 leaves at the beginning and CAD 100 returns only after the stopping date. The cash-timing chart shows the return as a later reduction in cumulative outlay. It does not treat a possible future refund as money available for the upfront payment.

05

Compare flexibility without assigning it an invented investment return

The matrix combines four stopping dates with four refund assumptions. Positive values mean the annual plan costs less; negative values mean monthly billing costs less. Prices remain fixed. At a twelve-month stopping date, no time is unused, so changing the refund percentage has no effect.

Monthly billing retains cash for longer before later payments are due. That can matter to a household with competing bills or an uncertain income. This calculator does not attach an investment return to the retained cash, charge interest on borrowing for the annual fee or estimate the personal value of flexibility. Those factors would need explicit, separate assumptions.

A linear allocation by month also does not measure enjoyment. Someone might receive most of a service’s value in its first weeks, or pay for a membership they rarely use. The graphs compare cash prices and time covered. They do not establish whether the service is worthwhile or whether buying either plan improves the household’s finances.

06

Review the next charge as carefully as the first one

For an actual purchase, record the full price, included service, first payment date, minimum commitment, cancellation process and renewal date. Confirm when a cancellation takes effect and whether notice must arrive before a billing date. Replace the hypothetical refund with terms supported by the agreement and applicable local rules.

The model stops after one year and assumes no renewal. A real annual plan might renew automatically at a different price. A monthly plan might also have a minimum term that prevents the payment stopping when use stops. Either feature changes the comparison and should be placed on a dated schedule.

Use the charts to identify the duration and refund assumptions that make prepayment attractive, then check whether the upfront amount fits the cash budget. A lower equivalent monthly price is one part of that decision. The timing of the debit and the cost of stopping are part of the same commitment.
